name: Kurti
confidence_why: The only explicit statement, the SIL Kurti Organised Phonology Data checked by Bob Uebele (2002) after a decade of resident fieldwork, gives non-contrastive stress always on the final syllable and no published source disagrees; the sole counter-evidence is Blust's 1975 field wordlist from Liap, whose acute marks fall on the first syllable of several numerals and disyllables (rúweh, tóloh, háhuw, límweh, ónoh, kámwew, múdon) but on the last of others (sayát, sedé?, paláy, pohóy, edéy, paréy), raw, unanalysed and internally mixed.

Ms., 5 pp., PDF printed 26 August 2004. SIL Language & Culture Archives entry 42270 (posted 2011-09-13). Its bibliography cites Uebele & Uebele 1997 'Kurti Organized Phonology Data' and Uebele & Uebele 2002 'Phonology Essentials of the Kurti Language' (both mss, SIL Ukarumpa) and Beastley 1987 (ms, PBT Madang).

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is not phonemic and falls on the last syllable of the word, without exception according to the OPD.
new_statements.exceptions: None ('always'). The OPD separately notes /ii/ and /uu/ are geminate/double vowels rather than long vowels, and minor dialect differences between Sou village and the rest of Kurti (no stress difference mentioned). Caveat from primary data: Blust's 1975 Kuruti field transcriptions (RB2-011 p.320) carry acute marks on the penult in several disyllabic numerals (řúweh, tóloh, háhuw, límweh, ónoh) alongside final marks elsewhere (saŋát, sεdέ?, pohón, paréy), so the 'always final' claim is not independently corroborated.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain stated as 'the word'; OPD examples are citation forms including inflected verbs with subject prefixes (e.g. am.pa.har '2s+be careful'); no discussion of phrase-level prominence or clitics.
new_statements.identity_note: The OPD describes 'Kurti (Ndrukul) [KTM]', Ndramalmal area, Manus Province, villages Sou, Lomwei, Derimbat, Liap, Mundrau, Patlok, Wamandra, Mundripudeu, Pundru = Glottolog kurt1250 (alt. names Kuruti, Ndrugul). Text sample and checking done with speakers around Liap/Ndrompuhnuu; OPD notes minor dialect differences for Sou village. Blust's 1975 'Kuruti' packet is from Liap speakers, same variety. Do not confuse with Kele (kele1258) or Ere, closely related East Manus neighbours whose stress is described by Ross 2002.

readall_conflicts: For the record, two things already held by the project from the earlier reading bear on the question: (a) the SIL Kurti Organised Phonology Data (Uebele, checked 6 Dec 2002; line 147-148) says verbatim "Stress in Kurti is non-contrastive, and is always on the final syllable of the word." and is the basis of the catalog's fixed: final syllable record; (b) Blust's 1975 field notebook RB2-011 packet 22 'Kuruti' (Liap village; p. 320, jpg held by the project, which I viewed) is primary data with acute marks that are NOT uniformly final: numerals are marked non-finally (rúweh 'two', tóloh 'three', háhuw 'four', límweh 'five', ónoh 'six', also kámwew, múdon, náma?ay), while sayát '100', sedé? '1000', paláy, pohóy, edéy, paréy carry final marks. That notebook is not a stress statement and was not among the listed works, but it is a real tension with 'always final' that a human reader of the RB1-005 tape could settle. The tape itself remains inaccessible (UH login required).
